profile.behavior: Social and often colonial; flies over shallow water and plunge-dives for small fish and crustaceans, then gathers in flocks to rest on open shores.
field_marks: Shaggy black crown or rear crest, depending on season
Short black legs and dark eyes
Long pointed wings and a forked tail
profile.habitat: Warm coastal marine waters, especially shallow bays, lagoons, and estuaries; rests and nests on open sandy beaches and low-lying islands.

sources.title: Royal Tern Identification — All About Birds

findings: The primary specimen is identifiable as a Royal Tern and contains one head, one intact orange bill, two overlapping folded wings, two legs with webbed feet, and one forked tail. No unintended extra bird or attached supplementary part is present.

The long stout daggerlike orange bill, dark eye, white face and underparts, pale silver-gray upperparts, black rear crest, short black legs, pointed wings, and forked tail agree with the reference photographs and direct identification sources.

The depicted white forehead with a shaggy black rear crest is a valid nonbreeding or transitional adult pattern. Both Cornell and Audubon explicitly describe the seasonal recession of the black crown and retention of black at the rear of the head.

The detached wing and head/bill studies are clearly separated from the primary specimen. Their shapes and proportions are coherent with Royal Tern anatomy; neither bill looks truncated, reversed, or materially inconsistent with the other. Unequal mandible projection was not identified as a Royal Tern field mark by the checked sources.
The feet are somewhat stylized, but both retain recognizable black toes and interdigital webbing without a material duplication or structural impossibility.

All visible text was read in full. “Royal Tern,” “Thalasseus maximus,” “Laridae,” the habitat, behavior, six field-mark statements, palette, and all measurement strings are correctly spelled and contain no duplicated, omitted, substituted, or nonsensical wording.

The printed measurements—length 45–50 cm, weight 390–430 g, and wingspan 100–110 cm—exactly match Cornell’s published values. Audubon publishes a somewhat broader alternative range, but this does not invalidate the accurately attributed Cornell measurements.

The body-length ruler is internally consistent: 45 cm is at the bottom, 50 cm is at the top, values increase upward, and exactly four evenly spaced unlabeled interior ticks divide the range into five proportional segments. Its 45–50 cm endpoints match the printed length range, and the plate explicitly states “SCHEMATIC — NOT TO SCALE.”
The layout is legible and balanced, with the primary specimen visually dominant and the supplementary studies unmistakably detached.
No place name, ZIP code, coordinates, map, observation date, or other local-observation detail appears on the candidate plate.
